title: Fulani Militants Kill 14 Christians in Plateau State, Nigeria
summary: At least 14 Christians have been killed in fresh attacks across four local government areas of Plateau state, Nigeria, days after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu appealed for forgiveness over his failure
content: At least 14 Christians have been killed in fresh attacks across four local government areas of Plateau state, Nigeria, days after President Bola Ahmed Tinubu appealed for forgiveness over his failure to visit violence-affected communities during an earlier trip to the state and promised to rebuild destroyed communities and return internally displaced persons (IDPs) to their ancestral homes. The killings occurred between Sunday, Nov. 15, and Monday, Nov. 16, in Mangu, Riyom, Barkin Ladi and Bokkos local government areas, according to community sources and local security groups. Armed attackers reportedly targeted rural settlements and ambushed residents traveling between communities. The latest violence followed Tinubu’s visit to Jos on Saturday, Nov. 14, for an All Progressives Congress (APC) political rally at Zaria Road Stadium, where he acknowledged the suffering of communities affected by recurring attacks and displacement. Addressing residents and party supporters, Tinubu asked Plateau residents to forgive him for not visiting affected communities during his previous trip to the state in April. “When I last visited the other time, I was limited to the airport,” he said. “Forgive me if you didn’t see me in the hinterland, but I saw the devastation. I got the report from the governor. I saw horror in the faces of our people.” The president promised to rebuild communities destroyed by violence and facilitate the return of displaced residents. “We will rebuild your communities, and we will bring you back to your communities,” Tinbu added. “I have directed all the security agencies to take decisive action and sustain peace and stability on the Plateau.” He also commended the Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Dr. Bernard Doro, for identifying vulnerable populations and coordinating humanitarian assistance. Tinubu announced that 1,000 forest guards were undergoing training and that surveillance cameras promised to Plateau state had been procured to strengthen security monitoring and early warning operations. However, fresh attacks were reported within hours of the president’s departure from the state. In Mangu Local Government Area, armed attackers invaded Zwagal community in Jipal District at about 9 p.m. on Sunday, killing nine people. Other residents were reportedly missing following the attack. Silas Nanfwang, a resident who confirmed the incident to journalists, called on security agencies to intensify efforts to locate the attackers and bring those responsible to justice. In Barkin Ladi, 79-year-old Da Ishaku Pam Vwos was killed when armed men invaded Sho village at about 5:20 p.m. on Sunday, according to the Berom Youth Moulders Association (BYM). The association’s National Publicity Secretary, Rwang Tengwong, also reported the killing of 42-year-old Dauda John Davou during an attack on the Sambak community in Hoss District, Riyom LGA, at about 2 a.m. on Sunday. Another attack was reported in the Jol community around 12:10 a.m. on Sunday. According to BYM, local vigilantes responded to the attackers, preventing further casualties. The association said the incidents followed the shooting of Joshua Doro Dafwel in Jol on Wednesday. He is currently receiving medical attention. BYM also reported that Ina Arin was killed when armed men ambushed him and his friend, Abok Gyang, as they returned to Dorong village in Foron District. Gyang survived the attack. In Bokkos Local Government Area, two people, including a unit commander of the Plateau state-owned security outfit, Operation Rainbow, were killed in an ambush on Monday afternoon. The victims, identified as Gambo and his companion, were traveling on a motorcycle from Hurti village to Tadai in Manguna District when armed men attacked them at about 1:30 p.m. They had reportedly visited Hurti for a condolence visit and died at the scene. title: Can Women Be Deacons?

content: ABSTRACT: Whether or not women can serve as deacons is a live question for many Christians, especially with more churches shifting from a deacon-led to an elder-led polity. The nature of the role, the example of Phoebe, and the qualifications for deacons in 1 Timothy 3 may allow room for deaconesses, but each of these arguments faces compelling counterarguments. In the absence of clear biblical evidence for women holding this formal office, wisdom leads Christians to approach the question with both conviction and charity. For our ongoing series of feature articles for pastors and Christian leaders, we asked Benjamin Merkle (PhD, The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary), Research Professor of New Testament and Greek at Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary, to examine the biblical evidence for women serving as deacons. By asking the question “Can women serve as deacons?” we are not simply asking whether women can serve the church. Scripture obviously permits and commends women serving the church. The question is whether the New Testament permits women to hold the formal office of deacon. Many churches are asking this question, for at least two reasons. First, women should not be restricted from serving in places where the Bible does not restrict them. If the Bible permits women to be deacons, then a church’s tradition does not offer sufficient grounds to prohibit them from holding the office. Women are essential to the health and vitality of the church, and we certainly don’t want to limit the church’s effectiveness over an unbiblical practice. Second, many churches either have moved or are moving to a plural-eldership model of church leadership. Historically, many Baptist, baptistic, or nondenominational churches were governed by a board of deacons. These deacons held leadership authority in a way that many believe is inappropriate for the office of deacon. For complementarians, it would not be wise for women to be deacons in such a context since it would violate 1 Timothy 2:12 (“I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man”). Under complementarianism, the relevant question is not whether an office possesses any authority whatsoever, but whether an office’s authority constitutes the kind of teaching or governing authority restricted to men. If a deacon holds elder-like authority, then, regardless of the title used, it would be wrong for a woman to hold the position because she would have authority over a man. If, however, a church has male elders who have authority to lead the church, then some are asking if it would be permissible to allow women to be deacons since a deacon is a position with little to no authority. With hundreds of churches shifting from a deacon-led to an elder-led polity, the question of whether women can be deacons becomes relevant. This essay unfolds as follows. I present the three best views for allowing women to be deacons. 1 (I assume a complementarian framework. The egalitarian-versus-complementarian debate is important, but I will not address it here.) After presenting each argument in favor of women deacons, I provide counterarguments. Although there are reasonable arguments for allowing women to serve as deacons, this essay argues that the New Testament provides no clear text that permits women to hold the office of deacon. I conclude the essay with three principles to keep in mind when dealing with this issue in the local church. Argument 1: The Nature of the Office The first argument for allowing women to hold the office of deacon concerns the nature of the office itself: Deacons are servants and not leaders. 2 As servants, deacons do not possess authority but serve the church in low-key (though important) ways. Consequently, nothing in Scripture would prohibit women from holding this office. The elders (also called “overseers” or “pastors”) are given the task of teaching and leading the church. title: How to Beat Scrupulosity
summary: Scrupulosity questions whether we’ve done enough to please God. Pastor John offers a strategy for resisting intrusive thoughts and trusting Christ’s blood. Listen Now
content: Audio Transcript Welcome back to the podcast on this Thanksgiving week. Yesterday, we read about Jesus washing the feet of his disciples in John 13. Jesus worked his basin of water from disciple to disciple on the floor. When he reached Peter, Peter instinctively pulled his feet back and said, “You shall never wash my feet.” Then “Jesus answered him, ‘If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.’ Simon Peter said to him, ‘Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!’” Dump the basin on my head. Give me a shower! And then “Jesus said to him, ‘The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean’” (John 13:8–10). Peter is clean. He was chosen, and he was redeemed. Christ’s future work has already applied to him. Now he only needs his feet washed. Confessing sin is a part of daily cleansing (1 John 1:9), and that practice is never inconsistent with being “completely clean.” Peter is a living metaphor for justification and sanctification. And it tells me we can miss what Christ has done for us because we have dirt on our feet. We fixate on washing off the dust every day. We obsess over daily sanctification and forget that Christ washed us clean. Today on Ask Pastor John: how to beat scrupulosity. Today’s question is from a middle-aged man named Dave. “Pastor John, thank you for taking my question. I have struggled for many years with scrupulosity. That’s the word I learned last week while watching YouTube videos. When I looked up that word, scrupulosity, I wept for joy. My obsessive fears have destroyed my peace for many years. And I think I have discovered the root of most of my spiritual challenges and struggle with anxiety. So, now I want to ask you, Pastor John, what advice would you give to a man who has for years been paralyzed by scrupulosity?” There is a similarity between ordinary spiritual attacks that every believer endures, on the one hand, and more sustained obsessions that some believers endure, on the other hand. There’s a similarity. There’s an overlap. In other words, I don’t think we should overstate or understate the peculiar seriousness of what it is to deal with scrupulosity, or what is sometimes called obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Let me try to illustrate what I mean by the overlap between (1) the normal threat of a thought or an image or a behavior becoming an obsession that all of us experience and (2) the more persistent thoughts or images or behaviors that keep returning and returning, and won’t let a person have any rest, like a tick that bites you on the leg and sinks into your skin, and you try to pull it off, but it just grabs on deeper and harder. All of us deal with this danger. I’ve dealt with it personally and written about it, mostly in relation to sexual threats. For example, you inadvertently see some sexually riveting situation — say, a couple having sex on the ground behind your garage. Immediately, that image lodges itself in your consciousness with tremendous force. It threatens to take over. It wants to stay there and be developed in living color by your imagination. You can adapt this situation, this sexual temptation, to whatever your temptation is, whatever the threat of repetition is. You know the kind of thing I’m talking about. What do you do? Here’s my strategy. I’ll just sum it up quickly and then show how it might apply to this issue of scrupulosity. ANTHEM is my technique for handling a situation of threatening preoccupation with thoughts that ought not to be in my head. A: Avoid what triggers the thought or the image. If it’s inadvertent, don’t look back. If you can avoid the trigger in the first place, avoid it. N: Say no out loud to Satan, to your own mind. No — a strong, decisive no. “You will not have dominion over me (Romans 6:14)!” No to that thought, image, or memory. T: Turn your mind to another compelling reality. content: How often does church-leadership content online reveal a lightly veiled obsession with new ? The experts today might not come out and say it, but the assumption often seems to be: Surely after two thousand years and all of our light-year advances in technology, the church needs a serious upgrade. Capturing this sentiment, one article insists, “Church leaders face two options. Either battle the marketplace currents and strive to convince enough people to pay for sermon-centric Sunday gatherings, or rethink that model to better fit the realities of making disciples in the twenty-first century.” Someone recently shared a clip with me that illustrates one such updated model. The video features a popular preacher who begins his Sunday sermon by driving a Rolls-Royce onto a stage. Twenty-two screens surround him, and hundreds of light bulbs hang overhead. The “preacher” steps out of the half-a-million-dollar car and takes critics like me head-on: There are some of you who are saying, “Oh man, I can’t believe you drove a Rolls-Royce into church. Man, that’s gimmicky.” No, it’s not; it’s godly. “Oh, that’s trite. That’s flippant.” No, it’s from Christ’s playbook. If you ever go to church and you find yourself bored, blame the communicator, the pastor. Don’t blame God. Yeah, for some reason we go to church and expect boredom. Just the opposite should be true. We are — and this is going to mess you up — we are in the entertainment business. I agree that no one should be bored in church — and I certainly agree that God is not to blame for any boredom in the pews. This preacher’s gimmick implies, however, that the same old formula for church — prayer, singing, fellowship, preaching — can’t possibly keep the attention of modern people like you. Mere sermons won’t cut it. God needs us to spice things up. God is not surprised by our state-of-the-art technology or shriveling attention spans, and he has told us, from the beginning, what captures souls when we gather for worship. He’s told us how to do church, and his counsel hasn’t expired. A Church Anyone Would Want Do you want to hear about a church that was emphatically not bored? They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. And awe came upon every soul , and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common. And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved. (Acts 2:42–47) Don’t you want to be a part of a church like that? Don’t you want your local church to taste the camaraderie, sacrifice, growth, and joy these people experienced when they gathered? The God-authored recipe is remarkably simple and durable: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” What did this church do when it grew so wildly and unexpectedly? They gathered. They ate. They gave. They prayed. They preached. And because they devoted themselves to God’s inspired Sunday-service plan, they rejoiced and their numbers multiplied. It’s dumbfounding that we see this kind of church thrive for literally millennia and still conclude it’s time to shake things up. “Sunday sermons got us this far,” we say, “but we’ll take it from here.” What if God knew everything we know — artificial intelligence, fiber-optic internet, driverless cars, those new robot vacuums that can clean stairs — and deliberately told churches to pray, sing, eat, drink, and preach the word anyway? Preaching to Itching Ears God knew exactly what changes and pressures our churches would face in the twenty-first century, and so he warned us t

title: You Really Can Know Jesus
summary: Can we really know Jesus Christ? He may be high and lifted up, but seven fundamental truths make ongoing access to him possible. Watch Now
content: I have looked forward to this conference on “Knowing Jesus.” That theme is both awesome and scary. Awesome because, does it get any better than this? Knowing Jesus is at the very heart of reality, why we exist, why God made the world, what “education in serious joy” is for, what the gospel is for us. (“There is no greater thing,” as Graham Kendrick wrote in the song “Knowing Jesus” in 1993.) But it also could be scary because knowing Jesus is personal and spiritual-relational and enigmatic. We might think we know him until we pause and ask this: What does it mean to know Jesus? What’s it like? Do I really know him? I can imagine a few general orientations in this room. One group says, “I love Jesus. I know him; I commune with him regularly, even daily. Knowing and enjoying him is my life and joy. And oh, do I want to know him more! Any help I can get this weekend in sweetening my knowing and walking with Jesus, I’ll take it.” Another group says, “I think I know him. I say I know him. But do I really? I know about him. I’m in a church community where people talk freely about ‘knowing Jesus.’ But what really do they mean by this? How do you know someone you’ve never been in the same room with? How do you know someone if you’ve never seen their physical face and heard their physical voice or interacted with them in the way you do with a spouse or best friend? I think I know him, but I want to really know him — and know that I know him — and more often and more deeply enjoy the wonder of communing with him.” Then, a last group says, “I don’t know him. I know people who say they do, but I wonder, Do they? And whether they do or not, I don’t. If someone asked me, ‘Do you know Jesus?’ I would have to say, ‘I know some things about him, but I don’t know him, not like persons know persons.’” Some in this last category might even say, “I’m a Christian. I follow Jesus. I profess faith in Jesus. But if ‘knowing Jesus’ means anything like what it means to know other persons, then if I’m being honest, no, I don’t know him.” Our hope this weekend is that this theme and these four messages (and our concluding panel) have something to offer to each of these groups. And since our theme is “Knowing Jesus,” perhaps the greatest theme of all, my hope is that this weekend might truly be life-changing for you (whatever group you’re in), that something significant might be in the offing for your soul. And that some in this room would say, “I came in Friday morning knowing about Jesus, but not knowing Jesus. But now I know him.” Or: “Now I see in a whole new way what it means to know the risen Christ and walk with him.” I believe that, given this theme, today and tomorrow could make for a whole new day, a new era, in your life, and I want to begin our time by asking God for that. Father in heaven, be pleased to do that this weekend in this room. We don’t want to just know about Jesus. We want to know Jesus, and enjoy him, and have our souls and lives changed and shaped and directed and energized by him. Father, for those in this room who genuinely know your Son, make this weekend an occasion for knowing him more and going deeper with him. And for those who don’t know him, or know that they know him, make this a day of decisive change. We own that knowing your Son is not an achievement to be secured. It is a gift of your immeasurable grace to be humbly and gladly received. Open our minds and hearts to receive the offer of your outstretched hand in Jesus. Oh, may we know him and supremely enjoy him, and may it change everything for us. In Jesus’s name we pray. Amen. Where is Jesus right now? He’s not here. Not in body. There is a critical sense in which he is here in Spirit; we’ll come to that. But let me begin by recognizing the problem (so to speak) for knowing Jesus created by his ascension. Jesus was here. He dwelled among us. He taught and discipled. He died and rose. But now he’s not presently among us and physically accessible as he was for his d

content: When I turned forty, YouTube decided my body needed help — desperately. Advertisements regularly shouted warnings about my sagging arms, the creases etched into the corners of my eyes, and the coarse texture of my hair. Marketers promised products to smooth away my wrinkles, brighten my complexion, and shrink my soft midsection, all for the nominal sum of $24.95 a month. At first, I just rolled my eyes and groaned at these messages. But with each creak of my knees and new splotch on my face, the insecurities such ads churned up took root and burrowed deep. Perhaps I should cover my salt-and-pepper strands with boxed dye , I wondered. All the while, the onslaught of imperatives continued: Soften. Polish. Gloss. Tighten. Defy. Reverse. Godly Vision Such verbs don’t appear in the Bible. Scripture teaches us that “gray hair is a crown of glory” rather than something to moisturize, color, and conceal at all costs (Proverbs 16:31). But when social media scrutinizes our granny knees and wobbly bits, that picture of glory seems as elusive as the stamina we once enjoyed in our twenties. To be clear, the Bible doesn’t prohibit cosmetics or remedies. God clothes even the lilies of the field in beauty (Luke 12:27), and in his mercy, he provides medicine to relieve our pains (1 Timothy 5:23). But Scripture also teaches that our relationship with God far outweighs the transient beauty of shiny hair and supple skin. “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the L ORD is to be praised,” we read in Proverbs 31:30. As we age, how do we calibrate our vision to God’s? How do we look into the mirror, perceive every crevice, laugh-line, and blotch, and then respond with deeper joy in the one whose mercy has granted us every year and silvery strand? Sisters, here are four ways to view our changing appearance through the lens of heaven. 1. Embrace God’s Sovereign Design The world tells us our aging bodies are a problem to fix. Researchers expect the global anti-aging cosmetics market to exceed $90 billion within the next five years. The products driving this boom could stock a chemistry laboratory: retinoids, peptides, hyaluronic acid, niacinamide extracts, and ultraviolet light. Moisturizing and pigmenting aren’t enough; now, we need to restore the skin itself, halt cells in their decay, and command unraveling proteins to coil. Ironically, God engineers the very dimples and folds this multibillion-dollar industry seeks to abolish. Had our predecessors in the garden loved him with all their heart, soul, mind, and strength (Mark 12:30), anti-aging serums would reap zero profit. Our bodies, untouched by sin, would work, rest, nurture, and rejoice for all eternity without a single wayward hair or troublesome mole to concern us. But aging — the slow descent into physical death — is part of our God-given wages of rebellion (Romans 6:23). God has decreed that our return to the dust will involve thinning bones and aching backs (Genesis 3:17–19). Our hearts, pumping over a hundred thousand times each day, will thicken under the toil of prolonged service. Our muscles will melt away, and our joints will stiffen and throb. Our crooked backs and rotten teeth aren’t a cause for celebration, but the one who rules over them is. The Maker of heaven and earth is sovereign over every lax fiber and withered cell (Proverbs 16:4; Psalm 103:19). No molecule, protein, or cell spins outside of his control. When we consider God’s sovereign design behind every crevice and pockmark, we remember that he holds us in the palm of his hand (Psalm 31:15; Isaiah 49:16). For those who know Christ, there is no safer, more privileged place to be. 2. Remember Your Fleeting Nature Gray hair alerts us to our limited time on this earth. Apart from Christ, such reminders terrify, as they warn of the day when kings and beggars alike will plead for the mountains to hide them from judgment (Revelation 6:15–17). With the end in view, the world’s mad scramble to reverse aging
author: Kathryn Butler

content: It’s feasting season. Thanksgiving. Advent. New Year’s. But for Americans in particular, is there such a thing as a non -feasting season? Our society has a bizarre love-hate relationship with food, pulling the plate toward us with one hand while pushing it away with the other. On the one hand, about 40 percent of adults are clinically obese; on the other, more than one in eight adults rely on GLP-1 to suppress their appetite. We want food and we want to want food less. We struggle to break free from the clutches of Big Food, so we look to Big Pharma for help. Happy Thanksgiving? What’s the remedy for this gastronomic schizophrenia? As counterintuitive as it sounds, godly feasting provides an antidote to foolish gluttony. Feasting vs. Feeding The Bible has a lot to say about food, not just in isolated verses but in plot points central to the arc of Scripture. Many of the most egregious sins centered on food. For instance, the first sin involved rebellious eating, looking to something forbidden in search of goodness (Genesis 3:6). After the exodus, Israel grumbled about their desire for Pharaoh’s pots of meat (Exodus 16:3). Then, when the Lord provided manna in the wilderness, Israel reenacted the sin of Eve when they gathered food on the Sabbath against God’s command (Exodus 16:27–30). But the Bible also commends feasting, both spiritual and physical. Jesus offers himself as the bread of life, given for the nourishment of the saints in exile (John 6:35). And the church looks forward to a meal at the consummation of history, the marriage feast of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Between the resurrection and return of the Lamb, we weekly feast on his body and blood, anchoring our minds on what Christ has done and what Christ will do (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). Godly feasting leans into our place in between the times by remembering with gratitude what was and anticipating with joy what will be. All the blessed feasts in the Scriptures are communal celebrations . Something extraordinary has happened; raise a glass to the King! We shouldn’t eat what we regularly eat today; instead, “bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found!” (Luke 15:23–24). We break from feeding ourselves (simply giving our body what it needs) in order to feast (eating and drinking more than we need) as a blessed means of joyously celebrating the work of God in history. But most Christians rarely, if ever, truly feast with mindful gratitude. We just overeat. Spiritual Malnutrition “A companion of gluttons shames his father” (Proverbs 28:7). The glutton does not feast; his god is his belly. He looks for deliverance in his next snack, his next meal, his next drink. He does not fully grasp that man does not live by bread alone. He is not marked by gratitude. The emptiness in his soul, the purposelessness of his life, and the joylessness of his ease have taken root as a spiritual disease. “A glutton is one who raids the icebox for a cure for spiritual malnutrition,” Frederick Buechner observed ( Wishful Thinking , 35). Americans, overall, remain locked in a permanent state of pseudo-feasting. Our culture combines industrial-grade, highly addictive food products and dopamine-seeking, nihilistic joylessness. We mindlessly munch. Often, we hardly even taste or enjoy our food. (A 2026 JAMA study revealed 69 percent of kids and 78 percent of adults use screens while eating.) This is an often-undiscussed problem within the church. I don’t know any Christians who intend to be gluttonous. But I know many, myself included, who have at times felt buried by the shame that follows an episode or season marked by a lack of self-control. We know we cannot make peace with sin, but we aren’t sure what this specific path of repentance looks like. So, when believers recognize the shameful pattern, we try to restrict our calories or go on a diet, which doesn’t stick. We purge and we binge — godless,
author: Seth Troutt

title: A Maker’s Heart
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Holly Neal turned a lifelong love of creating into an unexpected opportunity to support sign language Bible translation.   The post  A Maker’s Heart  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Holly Neal loves people, and she loves making things. And when something catches her interest, she dives in. “I’m a maker,” she said simply. But making has become more than just a hobby for Holly. Through some of her family’s hardest seasons, it has offered them comfort and connection. And eventually it became an unexpected way to give back to what God is doing around the world. When Holly’s adult daughter Julia was being treated for leukemia, a friend invited them to learn how to quilt. The creative process gave Holly something to focus on as their family walked through a difficult season. It became a way to work through hard things alongside her daughter. Years later, when Holly’s grandson Graham was born during the COVID-19 pandemic, she reached for another familiar project: cross-stitching. Graham spent his first four months in the hospital. And because of visitation restrictions at the time, Holly spent long hours waiting in the cafeteria. So she brought her cross-stitch. Being busy helped calm Holly’s mind. Cross-stitching was a small, practical way to make the waiting a little easier. Holly and her husband, Steve, have continued to navigate some unique family circumstances as they’ve cared for their daughter and grandson. So when Chris and Lindsay Beals, Holly and Steven’s daughter and son-in-law, invited the couple to a Wycliffe event, they were especially excited. After a season of isolation, they looked forward to reconnecting with other Christians and hearing stories about what God was doing through Bible translation. One part of the work specifically stayed with Holly: sign language Bible translation. Curious about what sign language Bible translation actually looks like? See for yourself when you visit our interactive Bible Translation Experience! You’ll go on a global journey where you’ll meet some of the hardworking Deaf translators bringing the Bible to their people in a language and format that capture their hearts. Start your journey! → As a grandmother of a child with unique needs, Holly has a special place in her heart for communities and families who navigate specific challenges and contexts. Learning about the work of making God’s Word accessible to Deaf communities worldwide gave Holly a personal connection to a ministry she’d never fully understood before. Holly and Steve had already talked and prayed about a financial gift they wanted to make to Wycliffe. But as she continued thinking about the ministry and Bible translation projects for sign languages, another question kept coming to mind: “Steve and I had already come up with a number that we felt like to donate, but the Lord kept speaking to me. And I kept thinking, ‘But what can I do? … That’s our money, but how can I make an impact?’” So Holly began thinking about how much she had invested — in supplies, patterns, fabric and tools — over the years in her love of crafting. She wondered if some of those things could become part of her gift to Bible translation. And what if Holly passed some of those supplies along to other makers and used the proceeds to support Bible translation for sign languages? See how one couple in Alabama also creatively used their gifts and skills to give back to Bible translation → Giving in Community Holly decided to hold what the stitching community calls a “destash” — an opportunity for her to sell supplies she already owned to other stitchers who could put them to good use. She shared the idea through her YouTube channel and social media, where she had already connected with a community of people who love cross-stitch. So when Holly told her stitching community about Wycliffe and her desire to support sign language Bible translation, she invited them into partnering with something that mattered to her. And people responded with generosity! Some people paid more for supplies and projects than the asking price, wanting to give a little extra toward the cause. title: Discipling Your Child’s Heart (A Chat with Melissa Paredes)
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Your church can help bring God’s Word to people still waiting. Wycliffe’s Scott Ross shares how prayer, service and initiatives like Adopt a Verse connect local congregations with Bible translation around the world.   The post  Discipling Your Child’s Heart (A Chat with Melissa Paredes)  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: How old were you when you first learned that Jesus loves you? Perhaps you’ve always known it and can’t remember a day when you didn’t know the song “Jesus Loves Me” or couldn’t recite John 3:16 by heart. Maybe you were a teenager and learned about Jesus’ love through a friend or church summer camp. Or were in college and went to a concert where the gospel was clearly articulated. Maybe you were in the trenches of the workforce, and a coworker boldly shared with you about the God who radically changed their life. Regardless of how old you were, each of us who has chosen to follow Jesus has an origin story — a moment in our lives when the knowledge that “Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so” moved from head knowledge to heart belief. And from then on, our lives were transformed forever. This is the truth of the gospel and the power of understanding that Jesus loves you. People around the world are discovering the personal truth of John 3:16 for themselves in a language and format they clearly understand. Explore why understanding that “God so loved the world” transforms entire communities → A Changing Reality Throughout Christian history, the gospel has spread from one community to the next. Stories were told and retold, Scripture was translated, churches were planted, and discipleship deepened as people learned more about Jesus. Bible translation is foundational to all ministries of the church. It fuels evangelism, church planting, discipleship and more. It equips people to move from a blurry picture of who God is to a clear understanding and personal encounter with Jesus as Lord. Through Scripture, people are able to read, hear or see the love of God on display. Just two decades ago, most of the world’s language communities still needed Bible translation work to begin , let alone be completed. But praise God, in the last few years, we’ve seen tremendous progress made, with Bible translation underway in more languages than ever before . While the change in numbers is exciting, what’s more important is what they signify: Every number represents a person who has a story that matters to God. For these communities, the stories of future generations are being completely rewritten as children will now grow up never remembering a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. That statement bears repeating: There will now be people who never remember a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. From the first word of Genesis to the last word of Revelation, the Bible tells one incredible story: God’s love for the world and His invitation for people from every nation and language to know Him. Get a glimpse of how God continues writing this story today as more and more people are experiencing the power of His Word. Watch the video → A New Generation Growing Up With God’s Word Let’s take a look at some of the recent communities that are experiencing not only life transformation but generational transformation as they encounter Jesus personally through Scripture. Jakalteko | Guatemala The Jakalteko Bible was dedicated in July 2026 in Guatemala! During the celebration, John 1:1-18 was read aloud — a passage that focuses on Christ, the eternal Word and our Redeemer. Early on, many women in the community memorized Job 19 . Like Job, they had faced various hardships in their lives and identified with his suffering. title: Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Ken and Sally discovered a way to give God’s Word — a gift they’d had access to their whole lives — to others.    The post  Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: What did your journey to faith look like? Perhaps it was a story of how God showed up in the midst of uncertainty, doubt or fears. Maybe it involved Him seeking you out and rescuing you. Or maybe you grew up in a Christian household and your story is a bit different — perhaps your family regularly read the Bible together and have always known about Jesus’ love. Ken Trager was raised that way. He reflected, “I think when you’re raised in a Christian home … and you have the routines of a life that is built around church and prayer, you just take it for granted.” He added, “It was just the air I breathed.” For Ken and his wife, Sally, faith was always part of their stories. They were each raised in Christian homes, followed Christ, got baptized and had parents who faithfully modeled church attendance, prayer and generosity.  Ken and Sally’s paths eventually crossed at Greenville University in southern Illinois, where they met and fell in love. They went on to build a life centered around family, faith and service. Ken spent his career as a teacher and coach while Sally worked as an accountant, and together they raised two children. Now retired, they’ve moved to be closer to their children and grandchildren, giving them a new opportunity to pour into the next generation. Through all those years and seasons, the faith Ken and Sally had seen modeled by their families continued to shape their home. Early in their marriage, Ken and Sally met a mentor who encouraged the couple to go deeper with their faith — to study Scripture, ask questions and wrestle honestly with what they believed. It was an important season of discovering that the faith that had been passed down from their families could also become something they personally owned and lived out together. What Do You Take for Granted? Years later, the couple experienced an aha moment when they were introduced to Wycliffe at an event. There, Ken and Sally heard story after story from people who had received Scripture in their own languages. Something clicked for Sally: “We’ve never known a day where we couldn’t access the Bible. And these people have just longed for it, and they’re finally getting it.” For the first time, something that had always surrounded the couple became visible — and it was a gift they could no longer take for granted . Ken and Sally had spent years thinking about the importance of God’s Word. Seeing people receive Scripture in their own languages helped them understand just how extraordinary that access is. “The power of salvation comes through that,” Ken said. “I can’t think of … [a more] important work than providing God’s Word to everybody in the world.” Sally agreed. “To have His Word is as if we’re hearing the voice of God,” she said. “God works through His Word.” This conviction — for people around the world to be able to access Scripture for themselves — became one of the reasons Ken and Sally prioritized a place in their giving for Wycliffe. But it also became part of a larger question about generosity they had been asking themselves for years: “If everything we have is a gift from God, what does it look like to live generously with it?” A Generous Heart Generosity, like faith, was something Ken and Sally had grown up around. Ken remembers his dad giving him money to put in the offering plate, and Sally remembers watching her parents give not just to their church but to people and organizations in need. Sally’s father especially enjoyed giving anonymously. As Ken and Sally have grown older, they’ve learned that generosity isn’t simply about giving a certain percentage or checking a box; it’s about continually asking what it means to have a generous heart . For Ken, the question of what it means to be generous has become what he calls “Kingdom Advancement Giving.” When contemplating giving, he asks, “Is this going to advance the Kingdom for God’s glory?” That question has shaped the way the couple thinks about which individuals and organizations they

title: 5 Ways to Pray for Bible Translation Around the World
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Prayer is essential to Bible translation. Explore five specific ways to pray for local churches, translation teams and communities around the world.   The post  5 Ways to Pray for Bible Translation Around the World  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Before His ascension to heaven, Jesus called the whole Church to “go and make disciples of all the nations” ( Matthew 28:18, NLT ), a command often referred to now as the Great Commission. God’s plan was to build His Kingdom in and through the Church, including local churches in every corner of the globe. And that’s exactly what’s happening today! God is on the move, and His Spirit is being poured out upon the earth in ways we’ve never seen before, particularly in the history of Bible translation. For so long, the Church was viewed as having the deepest roots and strongest influence in the West, with the West sending out Bible translators to the farthest reaches of the world. But over the last half century, the Church has exploded, expanding South and East and shifting the landscape of Bible translation with it. Johnstone Ndunde, executive director of SIL Global, a key partner of Wycliffe’s, shared: “In the world where we serve, we have many churches that have discipled, educated people [who] are able to serve the Lord as well. God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” “God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” This is God’s hand at work. He desires for people from every language and community to experience His redemptive power through the blood of Jesus, leading to life transformation. Scripture in a language and format they clearly understand plays a vital role in that, enabling them to know God more deeply and grow through discipleship. Today, as the Great Commission is being advanced by the global Church, local churches are taking ownership and linking arms with Wycliffe and other Bible translation agencies around the world to ensure that their communities, countries and even entire regions have God’s Word. Prayer is foundational to seeing God’s Word translated and made accessible to every person still waiting. Whether you’re praying for local churches, translation teams or communities, your prayers matter. Here are five ways you can pray for Bible translation today: Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships Pray for Wisdom and Strength for Bible Translation Teams Pray for Deaf Communities to Encounter Jesus Through Sign Language Pray for More People to Join the Work of Bible Translation Pray for the Translation of the Full Bible 1. Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships As a result of missions and technology, the gospel has spread to more communities than ever before, and now local churches worldwide are rising up to establish evangelism, discipleship, church planting and other activities in their own communities — with Bible translation central to all of those efforts! As local churches work with Bible translation organizations to translate Scripture for their own communities, that partnership is accelerating the pace of the work. This shift to local church ownership is a direct answer to decades of faithful prayer and service. Praise God! PRAY WITH US Heavenly Father, Thank You for how You are raising up men and women who not only love You but who want to be part of sharing the gospel in their own communities, countries and regions. Your love is capturing more people as they encounter You personally in a language and format they clearly understand. Equip local churches to spread Your light and love to their families and neighbors, drawing people to You through Scripture. Amen. Your Prayers Keep Us Going | The Philippines Divine Grace Leparto, a Bible translation field coordinator in the Philippines, shares the story of a translator who returned home from a weeklong Bible translation workshop to find that much of her land had been seized while she was away. Despite this difficult loss, she continued serving in Bible translation, grateful for the ways she could see the Lord at work in her community. Her experience is just one example of the challenges translation team members can face as the

title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. title: No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: See how Bible translation helps communities access more of God’s Word through print, audio and sign language Scripture today.   The post  No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Imagine reading a book, watching a show or listening to a podcast when suddenly the story just stops mid-sentence. Maybe the previous reader has ripped out a page, the series was canceled before the showrunners could wrap up the plotline, or the producer distributed the episode before realizing it was incomplete. How incredibly frustrating to not experience the full story from start to finish! It can leave us emotionally unsettled, frustrated or even distraught, because at our core, we desire completion. We want to know how things start and how they end. We don’t just want a taste, because it feels like a tease. We’re left wanting more . And we’re not alone in that desire! The same is true for communities around the world who are still waiting for the full counsel of God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. For some, they’re still waiting for the first verse of Scripture to be translated into their language. Others might have a few verses, chapters or Scripture portions . Still others are blessed with a complete New Testament but are waiting for the Old Testament so they can understand everything from Genesis to Revelation. They get a teaser of God’s great story — perhaps enough to understand who Jesus is and that He died for them — but they don’t have the full context as to why His sacrifice was so significant. The Bible changes everything, and together with our partners, Wycliffe believes that everyone should have access to the whole of Scripture. But don’t just take our word for it! Explore these Bible translation stories from our friends around the world who have personally experienced individual and community transformation as a result of encountering God through His Word. Want a glimpse of what it’s like to only have a portion of God’s Word? This “H ly B bl: Incomplete Scriptures” digital booklet helps you see what it’s like to have gaps in your understanding of the Bible. Explore the booklet → The Full “Outfit” of God’s Word Caroline always had access to a Bible growing up. But watching the Chonyi people of Kenya receive the New Testament in their language refreshed her passion for Bible translation, a mission she’s actively engaged in through SIL Kenya, a partner of Wycliffe. “They took a couple of Bibles, wrapped them up like a child,” she shared. “And there was a woman who was carrying the [Bibles]. And they were swinging and dancing, lifting up the [Bibles] and saying, ‘This is our child.’ Calling people, ‘Come,” in the Chonyi language. ‘Come and celebrate the child that has been born in us.’ “That is how the Chonyi people have taken the Bible — the New Testament — in their own language. That it is their child and they’re taking it seriously, making it bear fruit.” People gathered to hear Scripture read in their language, Bible studies began and the impact spread: 300 adults and 50 children gave their lives to Christ! At the celebration, the local pastors shared that now that the New Testament is complete, it’s like they have a shirt. But a shirt isn’t enough; they want a pair of pants (the Old Testament) to complete the outfit! Now work is underway to translate the Old Testament into Chonyi so that they can have the full “outfit” of God’s Word. Praise God! Watch how the Chonyi community celebrated the dedication of the New Testament in their community! As her neighbors listened alongside her, they became captivated by the story of Jesus. One day, someone from the community called the local translation office with a request. “We have been enjoying this Jesus story from this elderly woman, and now it has broken. title: ‘Only the beginning’ for IMB ministry partner in South Asia
summary: The conversation began on a dusty road in rural South Asia. Siraj, a Christian, told Derrick Waters about his desire to share the gospel with Muslims. How could he begin discussions about Christ with his neighbors? After months of training and encouragement, Siraj said, “I will soon share the gospel with 100 Muslims. I know that at least a few will believe.” Waters and his wife, Rosemary, are International Mission Board missionaries who serve in South Asia. His connection with Siraj is a breakth
content: IMB missionary Derrick Waters spent many days in areas like this market, learning his mission field. He made a breakthrough when he met Siraj, who now confidently shares the gospel. IMB Photo The conversation began on a dusty road in rural South Asia. Siraj, a Christian, told Derrick Waters about his desire to share the gospel with Muslims. How could he begin discussions about Christ with his neighbors? After months of training and encouragement, Siraj said, “I will soon share the gospel with 100 Muslims. I know that at least a few will believe.” Waters and his wife, Rosemary, are International Mission Board missionaries who serve in South Asia. His connection with Siraj is a breakthrough in sharing the gospel in this strongly Muslim region. When he first arrived on the mission field, Waters spent his early days getting acclimated to his new community by riding on the back of a motorcycle with a national partner, traveling around and making contacts. “My partner was trying to convince me not to buy a helmet because he said he was a safe driver,” Waters said, though he chose to wear the headgear. “It’s a good thing I wore the helmet because he drove into the back of a truck with a metal bar hanging out that smacked my head.” Surviving the motorcycle ride led to the relational network that eventually allowed Waters to meet Siraj. After they connected, Siraj introduced Waters to Muslim friends and watched him share the gospel. “At first, that’s how it was with Siraj,” Waters said. “But what I really wanted was for him to get involved in the work himself.” A few months later, Waters and local ministry partners traveled to Siraj’s village to lead evangelism training. They discussed God’s love for all people, learned key vocabulary and practiced a straightforward way to share personal testimonies and the story of Jesus. Then came the hard part. Waters began asking Siraj to lead conversations. Siraj stumbled through explanations and searched for the right words. He sprinkled in newly learned terms and nervously worked through the gospel message. Slowly, confidence replaced fear. After another season of ministry together, Siraj told Waters something he would never forget. “Before you came, I didn’t know how to share the gospel with Muslims,” Siraj said. “I wanted to, but I didn’t know how. Now I feel like I can do it.” The transformation became visible during a gathering arranged by a local teacher. Dozens of parents assembled to listen. Siraj stood before them, visibly nervous. His first few sentences faltered. He started, stopped and restarted. Then, something changed. Finding his rhythm, he shared what he had learned, speaking clearly and naturally. He used the vocabulary he had practiced and explained the message of Jesus with growing confidence. By the end of the meeting, the listeners invited the believers to pray for sick family members. They served snacks and chai, thanked them for coming and invited them back. For Waters, it was a glimpse of what God could do through one willing believer. Today, Siraj continues learning and sharing. He studies from a Bible in the local language that helps him engage more effectively with Muslim friends. He distributes Bibles, shares the gospel with coworkers and regularly speaks with people in the villages. This house is part of the village where Siraj lives with his wife, three daughters and his mother. He supports them on the equivalent of US$4 a day, while also farming his land and studying to earn his Ph.D. IMB Photo His enthusiasm is especially remarkable considering his circumstances. Siraj supports his wife, three daughters and his mother on the equivalent of US$4 a day. He farms a small plot of land and studies for exams in hopes of pursuing a Ph.D.  Despite these responsibilities, he continues making time to tell others about Christ. title: A Thanksgiving in Poland to remember
summary: For Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their family, Thanksgiving is more than a cherished American holiday. Living and serving in Poland as International Mission Board missionaries, it has become one of their most effective opportunities to build relationships, share their culture and ultimately point people to Christ. While Poland celebrates Christmas and Easter on a grand scale, Thanksgiving is uniquely American. Many Poles are familiar with the holiday and curious about its traditions. Over the years,
content: In 2018, God provided food for more than 70 people, double the expected number, at a Thanksgiving celebration Cal and Erin Hiebsch helped to host in order to share the gospel by telling the story of God’s provision for the Pilgrims on the first Thanksgiving. IMB Photo For Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their family, Thanksgiving is more than a cherished American holiday. Living and serving in Poland as International Mission Board missionaries, it has become one of their most effective opportunities to build relationships, share their culture and ultimately point people to Christ. While Poland celebrates Christmas and Easter on a grand scale, Thanksgiving is uniquely American. Many Poles are familiar with the holiday and curious about its traditions. Over the years, the Hiebsch family has learned to use that curiosity as a bridge for ministry. “Thanksgiving is probably one of our bigger entrées into American culture,” Cal explained. Each year, they invite friends, neighbors and participants from their English conversation clubs to experience a traditional Thanksgiving meal. For many guests, this is their first encounter with foods such as stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potato casserole and roasted turkey. Even finding a whole turkey in Poland can be a challenge, since stores more commonly sell turkey breasts and other cuts rather than the whole bird. One Thanksgiving, in particular, is especially memorable for the family. With the help of volunteers, Erin and the culinary crew carefully planned a special celebration. “We had people in four or five different kitchens across the city cooking,” she said. A generous spread of traditional American dishes filled the tables, and invitations had been extended throughout their community. Based on past events, they expected 20 to 30 people to attend. Erin said they planned for “double batches” of each dish with the intention of everybody trying a little of everything that was served. Servers fill up plates as IMB missionaries Cal and Erin Hiebsch and their friends host a Thanksgiving meal in Poland. They planned for 20 or 30 people to show up, but nearly 70 people filled the house. Thankfully, everyone had a full meal and heard the gospel message. IMB Photo As the evening began, guests kept arriving. More came through the doors. Then more. Soon the room was packed. Instead of the anticipated crowd of a few dozen, nearly 70 people showed up. The gathering became standing-room only. “I quietly asked a couple of the volunteer ladies to be praying that there would be enough for everyone,” Erin recalled. Cal was serving as emcee for the event, welcoming guests and sharing the Thanksgiving story. Meanwhile, others were distributing plate after plate of food. Every time someone entered the room, the challenge seemed to grow. How could the food possibly stretch far enough? Yet somehow, it did. People continued to receive full plates. Everyone ate. Conversations flourished around the tables. “The pumpkin pie was especially popular,” Erin said. Guests learned about the history of Thanksgiving and heard how God had provided for the Pilgrims during difficult circumstances. Most importantly, they heard the gospel woven naturally into the evening’s program. When the event finally concluded, the team compared notes and realized an astonishing experience occurred. “We doubled our crowd and had enough food for everyone to have a good Thanksgiving feast,” Cal recalled. To this day, Cal and Erin still talk about that evening. The experience remains difficult to explain, outside of God’s provision. They prepared for one number of guests and served more than twice as many. Whether miraculous or simply an extraordinary provision, the outcome was undeniable. More people than expected were welcomed, fed and exposed to the hope of Christ. An American holiday became a platform for meaningful conversations and gospel witness in a place far from home. title: First Person: Why we ask you to pray
summary: My husband and I moved from our home in Tennessee to South Asia when we were in our 20s. God called us to serve overseas through the International Mission Board, and we were excited to share the gospel with those who had not yet had an opportunity to hear it. As we began to plant our lives in a city on the other side of the world, we quickly realized the task before us was massive. We were surrounded by millions of people, the vast majority of whom were spiritually lost and on a trajectory to an
content: April Bunn, IMB director of global prayer strategies, shows messengers at an SBC annual meeting the latest Loving the Lost prayer resource. IMB Photo April Bunn directs global prayer strategies for the IMB. IMB Photo My husband and I moved from our home in Tennessee to South Asia when we were in our 20s. God called us to serve overseas through the International Mission Board, and we were excited to share the gospel with those who had not yet had an opportunity to hear it. As we began to plant our lives in a city on the other side of the world, we quickly realized the task before us was massive. We were surrounded by millions of people, the vast majority of whom were spiritually lost and on a trajectory to an eternity separated from Christ. We were grappling with a new language, a different culture, unfamiliar foods, homesickness and the list went on. We were overwhelmed. The reality of the lostness around us felt too much to carry. As we turned to God for help, He reminded us that we were not meant to carry this task alone. We had been sent as laborers to the nations, but the Great Commission was given to the whole Church. The Church was our partner in this work. As we began intentionally inviting brothers and sisters in the U.S. to walk with us regularly in prayer, we saw God move in unmistakable ways. They carried the burden of lostness with us, and they also rejoiced with us as we saw God work. We had been sent as laborers to the nations, but the Great Commission was given to the whole Church. The Church was our partner in this work. Today, after two decades in South Asia, I have the privilege of encouraging and equipping believers to pray for people and places around the world through my work with the IMB. In doing so, I’m continually reminded that God’s mission is His work, and we are utterly dependent on Him to accomplish it. Missionaries can faithfully go, learn languages, share the gospel and disciple believers, but they cannot change hearts. God can. That is why we ask you to pray. Prayer is strategic to the Great Commission, and e very believer can take part in it. As the Church, we are living between the giving of the Great Commission and its culmination in the great multitude we see in Revelation 7:9, where people from every nation, tribe, people and language will stand before the throne worshiping God together. Until that day, we go to take the good news to a world in need. And we pray, asking God to do what only He can do. Through prayer, every believer, regardless of age or location, can intercede for places we may never be able to go ourselves. No country or people group is closed to the work of the Spirit through the prayers of God’s people. We may not see every answer to those prayers in our lifetime; some will only become visible when we stand before the throne and see the faces of those God drew to Himself. Until then, we keep praying. April Bunn, IMB director of global prayer strategies, shows messengers at an SBC annual meeting the latest Loving the Lost prayer resource. The new Loving the Lost is available for free from the IMB. IMB Photo Paul tells us in Colossians 4:2 to “continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.” To be watchful means we are paying attention and expecting God to work. The Mixtec people of Mexico have reminded me what that kind of watchful, steadfast prayer looks like. Beginning in 2008, IMB missionaries serving among the Mixtec began sharing prayer requests with IMB’s prayer office so they could be shared widely and more believers could join them in prayer. The requests were simple. Pray for open hearts. Pray for opportunities to share Bible stories in the Mixtec language. Pray for people to help make Scripture accessible. Pray for God to open doors. Month after month and year after year, people prayed for access to villages, for the first believers, for courage in the face of persecution. Today there is a growing fellowship of Mixtec believers. content: An IMB missionary among the Deaf records a Bible story in sign language. IMB Photo Every dollar you give to the Lottie Moon offering goes to support missionaries like Noah Lewis who live and serve among the lost. Will you consider giving today? Noah Lewis couldn’t help signing along with a worship song playing in the background as Deaf friends gathered in his home for dinner. The International Mission Board appoints missionaries who are both Deaf and hearing to serve among the global Deaf. Many missionaries learn sign language for the first time, while others use their American Sign Language to more quickly learn global sign languages. IMB Photo The International Mission Board missionary was sitting in the living room with his roommate and two friends while others prepared food nearby. As a young, single adult, simply opening the doors to his home in the Middle East has created some of his most fruitful opportunities for gospel conversations. That evening, Lewis was stirred to worship the Lord. “I just love worshiping in sign language because it’s a full-body experience,” Lewis said. Lewis, who is hearing, began signing the song in American Sign Language. Across the room, one of his Muslim friends watched intently. When the song ended, his friend told him it was beautiful and asked to see another. Lewis explained that Christians use songs to worship God. His friend compared what he had seen to hearing the Islamic call to prayer. The exchange opened an opportunity for Lewis to explain Christian worship and why Christians worship Jesus. When his friend asked to see more, Lewis continued signing songs from the playlist. “He was just really captivated by it,” Lewis said. “It really felt like in that moment the Spirit was working in his heart.” The conversation did not end with a profession of faith. Instead, it became another step in a friendship where Lewis has watched spiritual curiosity grow over time. During Ramadan, the same friend asked about fasting. On another night, he asked how Christians pray. Each question has allowed Lewis to explain what Christians believe and why he follows Jesus. Those conversations reflect much of Lewis’ ministry. He has served in the Middle East for nearly a year and a half, spending much of his time learning sign language and building relationships in the local Deaf community. Learning sign language, like learning any language, requires time, practice and immersion in the community that uses it. For Lewis, that process has looked different from the experience of missionaries who can spend several hours each day in a formal language school. There are no comparable sign language centers where he serves, so much of his language learning happens through relationships with Deaf friends. Although Lewis has not had a dedicated language tutor since arriving on the field, personal relationships help him develop a strong conversational understanding of the sign language used where he serves. The process has also drawn him more deeply into the Deaf community he came to reach. “I want to genuinely learn about their language,” he said. “I want to be friends with them. I want to know who they are.” As Lewis’ ability to communicate grows, relationships deepen and opportunities to share the gospel follow. Even when he doesn’t know the exact sign he needs, friends help him find ways to communicate biblical truths. Lewis has learned to faithfully use the language he has while continuing to grow in his ability to communicate the gospel clearly. An IMB worker among the Deaf records a Bible story. Generous giving to the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering supports missions among the global Deaf. Lewis currently lives and serves in the Middle East, but he arrived on the field with a long-term desire to serve in Central Asia. content: Participants at the IMB Sending Celebration on Nov. 9, 2026, celebrated God's faithfulness in sending 33 new missionaries to the nations. Held at the Sugarcreek campus of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, the event launched the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio annual gathering. For security reasons, some newly appointed missionaries are not publicly identified. IMB Photo God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sending and sustaining those called by God to go to the mission field. Senior Pastor Chad Keck welcomed those in attendance, sharing his appreciation for the partnership with Southern Baptist churches to cooperatively send and support missionaries. The Sending Celebration is meeting in conjunction with the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio. Chad Keck, senior pastor of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, left, and Jeremy Westbrook, executive director-treasurer of the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio, right, welcome guests gathered for the IMB Sending Celebration, which kicked off the convention’s annual gathering. IMB Photo Among those who shared their stories include a couple who answered an unexpected call later in life, a couple who are returning to Albania and to people they could not forget; and a couple who moved from welcoming the nations in Canada to going to Fiji. All of them shared their stories before the Sending Celebration. Unexpected invitation to go On Dec. 5, 2025, what seemed like an ordinary FaceTime call became a turning point for Rob Boss. As he spoke with his daughter, Hannah, during her IMB training, Rob sensed God speaking clearly to his heart: “You can do this too.” The impression was unexpected. After decades of writing, Christian education, seminary teaching and active support of missions, overseas service had never been part of Rob and Stephanie Boss’ plans. “It wasn’t an audible voice, but it was so clear,” Rob said. “It was Him. It was so kind and so gentle and so encouraging.” The moment drove him to his knees in surrender. When Stephanie came home later that day, he told her he believed God was calling them to the nations. Her response was immediate. “Thrilled is the right answer,” she said. The next day, the couple contacted the IMB and began the application process. Though missions had long been part of their family’s story, Rob and Stephanie Boss sensed God leading them to overseas service while encouraging their daughter, Hannah, during her missionary training. Sent by Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, Texas, they are now headed to Colombia, where they will serve through theological education. IMB Photo Looking back, the Bosses see the Lord’s hand preparing them long before they realized where He was leading. “God brought us together in the summer of 1990 at Glorieta, New Mexico, where we met and married,” Stephanie said during the Sending Celebration. What followed was years of ministry, teaching, parenting and navigating life’s unexpected turns, which taught them to hold plans loosely and trust God completely. “We did not have a clue about what life held in front of us,” Stephanie said. “We just knew we wanted to follow the Lord.” Their calling also continues a family legacy. Rob’s mother served with the IMB in Africa after retirement, helping inspire Hannah’s service in South Korea. Now, three generations of the same family have answered God’s call to the nations. title: IMB missionaries in place, prepared to encourage Senegal’s churches toward Youth Olympics outreach
summary: As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is exting
content: A Senegalese Christian shares the gospel with event volunteers during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is extinguished. “This is the first Olympic event ever held on the continent of Africa,” West said. “For us, it was an opportunity to ask, ‘What are we going to do with this?’” The Youth Olympic Games, which began Oct. 31 and end Nov. 13, are taking place across three host cities: Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. Event organizers expect nearly 2,700 athletes, ages 14-17, to participate in 35 sports and represent more than 200 delegations. The Games have drawn a million spectators, and West reported more than 6,000 event volunteers are staffing all the venues. With so many people gathering in Senegal, West and his team concentrated on preparing Senegalese churches for evangelistic opportunities. “We could run and hide, or we could do this thing,” West said, recalling an early conversation with teammates. “We decided we were going to do this thing.” The 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, is the first Olympic event held on the continent of Africa. IMB Photo West serves as team leader for IMB work in Senegal, where ministry efforts focus on three areas: gospel engagement, church advancement and community development. The Youth Olympic outreach naturally aligns with the first two priorities. “Our approach has been to mobilize the local church,” he said. “This is their backyard.” Instead of relying on a large influx of international volunteers, though there is one volunteer team from the United States serving, the strategy has centered on equipping local believers. Senegal has four Baptist churches in the greater Dakar area. Many leaders representing the congregations, as well as other ministry partners, participated in evangelism training designed specifically for the Games. Church leaders and ministry partners in Senegal participate in an evangelism training session specifically designed to share the gospel during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo A key outreach method involves trading commemorative pins, a familiar Olympic tradition. Volunteers use the exchange as a natural conversation starter before offering gospel-centered materials. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code connected to a digital engagement platform adapted from previous Olympic and World Cup outreaches. Visitors who scan the code are directed to online resources and can connect with trained digital responders. Experienced volunteers in the U.S. are helping provide follow-up conversations. “We’re building on strategies that have been used effectively in previous Olympic Games,” West said. “It’s an easy, non-intimidating way to start gospel conversations.” Trading commemorative pins is an Olympic tradition. Volunteers use these pins to start gospel-driven conversations during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code that connects people to trained digital responders. IMB Photo The effort extends beyond Dakar. IMB teams and church partners are positioned in each of the three host cities. An IMB team, which includes three global missionary partners, is helping coordinate outreach efforts in Diamniadio, and an IMB team along with a Baptist church is organizing efforts in Saly. West believes the greatest potential impact may be felt not among international visitors but among Senegalese believers themselves. Senegal is approximately 95% Muslim and 0.2% evangelical.
